blocks.text: Consider a circuit consisting of a battery of emf ε connected in series with a resistance R (Fig. 9.23). A steady current I flows through the circuit and a steady potential difference V exists between the terminals A and B of the resistor R. Terminal A, connected to the positive pole of the battery, is at a higher potential than the terminal B. In this circuit the battery is continuously lifting charge uphill through the potential difference V. Using the meaning of potential difference, the work done in moving a charge Q up through the potential difference V is given by
This is the energy supplied by the battery.
The rate at which the battery is supplying electrical energy is the power output or electrical power of the battery. Using the definition of power, we have

blocks.text_alt: Electrical power = Energy supplied/Time taken = V Q/t

blocks.text: The above equation can also be written as:

blocks.alt: A rectangular circuit: a battery E on the left side with + at the top, a resistance R on the right side between terminal A (top) and terminal B (bottom), and an arrow I along the top wire pointing right. A dotted double arrow V in the middle spans from top to bottom.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.23: The power of a battery appears as the power dissipated in the resistance R (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.23).

blocks.text: Equation 9.39 is a general relation for power delivered from a source of current I operating on a voltage V. In the circuit shown in Fig. 9.23 the power supplied by the battery is expended or dissipated in the resistor R. The principle of conservation of energy tells us that the power dissipated in the resistor is also given by Eq. 9.39.
Alternative equation for calculating power can be found by substituting V = IR, I = V/R in turn in Eq. 9.39.

blocks.latex: P = V \times I = IR \times I = I^2R
blocks.text_alt: P = V × I = IR × I = I²R

blocks.latex: \text{or} \qquad P = V \times I = V \times V/R = V^2/R
blocks.text_alt: or   P = V × I = V × V/R = V²/R

blocks.text: Thus, we have three equations for calculating the power dissipated in a resistor.

blocks.latex: P = V \times I, \qquad P = I^2R, \qquad P = V^2/R \qquad (9.40)
blocks.text_alt: P = V × I,   P = I²R,   P = V²/R   (9.40)

blocks.text: If V is expressed in volts and I in amperes, the power is expressed in watts.
